Pin.definition: A piece cannot or should not move because a more valuable piece (or the king) sits behind it on the same line. Absolute when the king is behind it.

Skewer.definition: The reverse of a pin: a valuable piece is attacked and forced to move, exposing a lesser piece behind it.

Fork.definition: One piece attacks two or more enemy targets at once; at least one usually cannot be saved.

Double Attack.definition: Two threats created in a single move, more than the opponent can meet.

Discovered Attack.definition: Moving one piece unveils an attack from a piece behind it.

Discovered Check.definition: A discovered attack where the unveiled line gives check, freeing the moved piece to do anything.

Double Check.definition: Two pieces give check at once; the king must move.

X-Ray.definition: A piece exerts influence through an enemy or friendly piece along a line.

Deflection.definition: Forcing a defending piece away from a key duty.

Decoy.definition: Luring a piece (often the king) onto a bad square.

Attraction.definition: Forcing an enemy piece onto a square where it can be hit by a follow-up.

Clearance.definition: Vacating a square or line so another piece can use it, often with tempo.

Interference.definition: Interposing a piece to cut the line between an enemy piece and what it defends.

Removing the Defender.definition: Capturing or chasing the piece that guards a key square or unit.

Overloaded.definition: A piece with too many defensive duties; loading it further breaks something.

Zwischenzug.definition: An in-between move (often a check or threat) inserted before the 'expected' recapture.

Windmill.definition: A repeating discovered-check mechanism that harvests material.

Desperado.definition: A doomed piece grabs whatever it can before it is lost.

Battery.definition: Two pieces lined up on the same file, rank, or diagonal to multiply pressure.

Greek Gift.definition: The Bxh7+ (or Bxh2+) bishop sacrifice to open the enemy king.

Sacrifice.definition: Giving up material for attack, initiative, structure, or mate.

Exchange Sacrifice.definition: Giving up a rook for a minor piece to gain positional or attacking value.

Trapped Piece.definition: A piece with no safe squares, about to be won.

Loose Piece.definition: An undefended piece — 'loose pieces drop off.'

Hanging Piece.definition: A piece that can be captured for free or wins material for the attacker (SEE > 0).

Attack.definition: A direct threat against a piece, square, or the king.

Check.definition: A direct attack on the king that must be answered immediately.

Forcing.definition: Checks, captures, and threats that sharply limit the opponent's replies.

Put Pressure on the Pinned Piece.definition: Piling attackers onto a pinned unit that cannot flee.

Back-Rank Mate.definition: Mate on the back rank by a rook/queen against a king boxed in by its own pawns.

Back-Rank Weakness.definition: The king's back rank lacks a luft escape, inviting back-rank tactics.

Smothered Mate.definition: A knight mates a king hemmed in entirely by its own pieces.

Arabian Mate.definition: Rook and knight coordinate to mate a cornered king.

Anastasia’s Mate.definition: Knight and rook mate a king trapped on the edge.

Boden’s Mate.definition: Two bishops on crossing diagonals mate a castled king.

Epaulette Mate.definition: The king is mated flanked by its own pieces blocking escape.

Hook Mate.definition: Rook, knight, pawn and enemy pawn combine to mate on the edge.

Ladder Mate.definition: Two rooks (or queen+rook) drive the king up the board rank by rank.

Dovetail Mate.definition: Queen mates a king whose two escape squares are blocked by its own units.

Mating Net.definition: A web of threats from which the king cannot escape.

Smothered.definition: King's escape squares are all occupied by friendly pieces.

Stalemate.definition: No legal move while not in check — a draw.

Zugzwang.definition: Any move worsens the position; the obligation to move is the problem.

Opposition.definition: Kings face off with an odd number of squares between; the side NOT to move holds the opposition.

Triangulation.definition: Losing a tempo with the king to hand the opponent the move (zugzwang).

Underpromotion.definition: Promoting to knight/rook/bishop for tactical or stalemate-avoidance reasons.

Promotion.definition: A pawn reaching the last rank becomes a piece.

Passed Pawn.definition: A pawn with no enemy pawns ahead on its file or adjacent files.

Connected Passed Pawns.definition: Two passed pawns on adjacent files supporting each other.

Protected Passed Pawn.definition: A passed pawn defended by another pawn.

Isolated Pawn.definition: A pawn with no friendly pawns on adjacent files.

Doubled Pawns.definition: Two friendly pawns on the same file.

Tripled Pawns.definition: Three friendly pawns on one file — a serious structural defect.

Backward Pawn.definition: A pawn behind its neighbours, unable to advance safely, often on a half-open file.

Hanging Pawns.definition: Two adjacent friendly pawns with no pawn support, strong but targetable.

Pawn Majority.definition: More pawns than the opponent on one wing.

Pawn Minority.definition: Fewer pawns on a wing, often used to launch a minority attack.

Minority Attack.definition: Advancing a pawn minority to create a weakness in the enemy majority (classic vs Carlsbad).

Pawn Break.definition: A pawn advance that challenges the structure to open lines.

Pawn Storm.definition: Rolling pawns forward to open the enemy king.

Pawn Island.definition: A connected group of pawns; more islands means more weaknesses.

Isolated Queen’s Pawn.definition: An isolated d-pawn (IQP): dynamic activity vs long-term weakness.

Carlsbad Structure.definition: The pawn structure from the Exchange QGD; theatre of the minority attack.

Maroczy Bind.definition: Pawns on c4 and e4 clamping down on d5 and the black position.

Stonewall.definition: A rigid pawn wall (d4/e3/f4 or ...d5/e6/f5) with a strong e5/e4 outpost.

Pawn Chain.definition: Diagonally linked pawns; attack the base.

Pawn Cascade.definition: A rolling sequence of pawn advances/exchanges.

Outpost.definition: An advanced square, pawn-supported and safe from enemy pawns, ideal for a knight.

Knight Outpost.definition: A knight installed on an outpost — often worth a rook's nuisance value.

Weak Square.definition: A square that cannot be defended by a pawn.

Strong Square.definition: A safe square from which a piece dominates.

Hole.definition: A permanent weak square in front of the pawns.

Space.definition: The territory controlled by advanced pawns; more space eases maneuvering.

Center.definition: The d4/e4/d5/e5 zone; control confers mobility and initiative.

Open File.definition: A file with no pawns; a highway for rooks.

Semi-Open File.definition: A file with only enemy pawns; pressure target.

Open Center.definition: Central pawns exchanged, favouring active pieces.

Closed Center.definition: Locked central pawns, favouring maneuvering and flank play.

Seventh Rank.definition: A rook on the enemy's second rank harasses pawns and king ('pigs on the seventh').

Long Diagonal.definition: The a1-h8 or a8-h1 diagonal, prime real estate for a fianchettoed bishop.

Fianchetto.definition: Developing a bishop to g2/b2/g7/b7 behind a knight-pawn.

Good Bishop.definition: A bishop whose pawns are mostly off its colour — free and active.

Bad Bishop.definition: A bishop hemmed in by its own pawns on its colour.

Two Bishops.definition: The bishop pair: a lasting edge in open positions.

Rook Behind the Passed Pawn.definition: Tarrasch's rule: rooks belong behind passed pawns.

Rook Lift.definition: Bringing a rook via the third rank into the attack.

Alekhine’s Gun.definition: Queen behind doubled rooks on a file — maximal pressure.

Color Complex.definition: Systemic weakness of squares of one colour (e.g., dark-square holes).

Prophylaxis.definition: Preventing the opponent's plan before pursuing your own.

Restriction.definition: Limiting the scope of enemy pieces.

Blockade.definition: Planting a piece in front of a passed pawn to stop it.

Maneuver.definition: Repositioning a piece to a better square over several moves.

Coordination.definition: Pieces working together toward one aim.

Piece Activity.definition: How much your pieces do; activity often trumps material.

Piece Mobility.definition: The number of good squares available to a piece.

Centralization.definition: Placing pieces (esp. king in the endgame) in the centre for maximum reach.

Domination.definition: Restricting an enemy piece so it has no good squares.

Compensation.definition: Non-material value (activity, structure, king safety) for sacrificed material.

Counterplay.definition: Active resources that offset the opponent's plans.

Initiative.definition: The ability to make threats and dictate play.

Tempo.definition: A unit of time; gaining a tempo means developing while making a threat.

Development.definition: Bringing pieces off the back rank into play.

Breakthrough.definition: Forcing open a closed position, often by pawn sac.

Infiltration.definition: Getting pieces into the enemy camp.

Penetration.definition: Invading via open lines to weak squares.

Simplification.definition: Trading pieces to reach a clearer or winning position.

Liquidation.definition: Exchanging into a known favourable endgame.

Transposition.definition: Reaching the same position by a different move order.

Move Order.definition: The sequence of moves, which can dodge or invite specific lines.

Conversion.definition: Turning an advantage into a win.

Keeping the Tension.definition: Declining to resolve a pawn/central tension to keep the opponent guessing.

Danger Levels.definition: Assessing how sharp/risky a position is before committing.

Overprotection.definition: Guarding a key point more than necessary to free the guardians.

Candidate Moves.definition: The short list of moves worth calculating in a position.

Calculation.definition: Concrete forward analysis of forcing lines.

Evaluation.definition: Judging who stands better and why.

Critical Position.definition: A turning point demanding precise play.

Quiet Move.definition: A non-forcing move that quietly strengthens a threat.

Waiting Move.definition: A move that passes the obligation to act to the opponent.

Horizon Effect.definition: Pushing a problem beyond the search depth so it seems to vanish.

Centipawn.definition: 1/100th of a pawn; the engine's unit of evaluation.

Evaluation Swing.definition: A sharp change in evaluation between moves or depths.

Blunder.definition: A serious error that changes the outcome (large centipawn loss).

Mistake.definition: An error that meaningfully worsens the position.

Miss.definition: Failing to play a clearly winning move or mate that was available.

Dubious.definition: A move of questionable soundness, playable but risky.

Novelty.definition: A new move in a known theoretical position.

Preparation.definition: Home analysis prepared before the game.

Book Move.definition: A move within established opening theory.

Theory.definition: The body of established opening/endgame knowledge.

Repertoire.definition: A player's chosen set of openings.

Sideline.definition: A less-common alternative to the main line.

Refutation.definition: A concrete demonstration that a move or line fails.

Poisoned Pawn.definition: A pawn that is dangerous to capture due to hidden compensation.

En Prise.definition: A piece left where it can be captured for free.

En Passant.definition: Capturing a pawn that just advanced two squares as if it moved one.

Touch-Move.definition: A touched piece must be moved if it has a legal move.

Swindle.definition: Saving a lost position by setting a trap.

Trap.definition: A tempting move that leads to trouble.

Hope Chess.definition: Making threats without checking the opponent's replies.

Practical.definition: Choosing what is easiest to play for a human, not necessarily objectively best.

Premature Attack.definition: Attacking before the position justifies it.

Counterattack.definition: Meeting a threat with a bigger threat.

Flank Attack.definition: An attack on the wings, best met by a central break.

Kingside Attack.definition: An assault on the enemy king's wing.

Queenside Expansion.definition: Gaining space and play on the queenside.

Castling.definition: King-and-rook move that tucks the king to safety.

Opposite-Side Castling.definition: Kings on opposite wings — a race of pawn storms.

Strategy.definition: Long-term planning based on position features.

Tactics.definition: Short-term forcing sequences to win material or mate.

Positional.definition: Play based on structure and squares rather than force.

Dynamic.definition: Play relying on activity, initiative, and time.

Static.definition: Enduring features like structure and material.

Unbalanced.definition: Asymmetric material or structure creating winning chances for both.

Gambit.definition: Sacrificing material (usually a pawn) in the opening for development or initiative.

Exchange.definition: A trade; also 'the exchange' = rook for minor piece.

Material.definition: The total value of the pieces.

Fortress.definition: A drawn setup the stronger side cannot break.

Dead Draw.definition: A position with no winning chances for either side.

King Safety.definition: How exposed the king is to attack.

Time Trouble.definition: Low clock time forcing fast, error-prone play.

Clock Management.definition: Budgeting thinking time across the game.

Opening.definition: The first phase: development, center, king safety.

Middlegame.definition: The fighting phase of plans and tactics.

Endgame.definition: Few pieces remain; king activity and pawns decide.

Accuracy.definition: How closely moves match the engine's best.

Depth.definition: How many plies ahead analysis reaches.

Human.definition: Pattern- and principle-based play under practical constraints.

Open.definition: Positions with open lines and piece play.

Diagonals.definition: Bishop highways; long diagonals are prime.

Files.definition: Vertical lines; rooks thrive on open ones.

Rank.definition: Horizontal lines; the 7th/2nd are attacking lanes.

Winning.definition: A decisive advantage with correct play.

Losing.definition: A decisive disadvantage with correct play by the opponent.

Lucena Position.definition: A winning rook-endgame technique ('building a bridge').

Tablebase.definition: Perfect precomputed results for positions with few pieces.

Rule of the Square.definition: Can the king catch the passed pawn? Check the pawn's square.
